You don't go knocking on Jamie Dimon's door, he doesn't understand what it is.
And, you know, eventually you will get to them, but in the early stages, the vendor financing thing is very normal.

quotes.text: The Federal Reserve will not sacrifice financial stability to accelerate its make-believe journey back to its arbitrary two percent inflation target after a half-decade plus of positive inflation surprises.
If the risk-off market regime condition deepens, the Fed will likely conclude this mid-cycle adjustment in December or conclude it in January at the latest.

We maintain conviction in our view that Ray Dalio's big-cycle framework specifically the disintegrating domestic political and geopolitical orders, Peter Turchin's elite overproduction framework, and Neil Howe, my friend, former colleague, and mentor, is fourth turning framework are each independent
The transition to a multipolar world order and resulting hit to the US dollar's reserve currency status simply does not square with the US cyclically and structurally deteriorating fiscal dynamics.
Foreign investors are likely to continue durably reducing their marginal demand for US dollar denominated assets over time.
If all these factors are true, then the biggest losers will be the companies whose balance sheets depend on slow depreciation of last generation chips.

key_points.point: The Federal Reserve will not sacrifice financial stability to accelerate its path to the two percent inflation target.
The risk-off market regime condition could deepen, leading the Fed to conclude its mid-cycle adjustment in December or January.
Geopolitical and domestic political order disintegration and elite overproduction are driving supply-demand imbalances in the Treasury Bond Market.
Foreign investors are likely to durably reduce marginal demand for US dollar-denominated assets over time due to deteriorating fiscal dynamics.
Companies whose balance sheets depend on slow depreciation of last-generation chips will be the biggest losers.

quotes.text: A concern of mine is that we are going to get a bunch of standard Fedspeak and that these task forces are just going to tell the Fed what they already know.
The Fed is somewhat unique. There are other central banks like the Bank of England last year that had a 441 vote, and that was considered okay.
I think it's more of a feature because part of the uncertainty that we're getting is not just because we're not getting specific Fedspeak, it's because we're getting uncertain data.
We're getting the Fed saying that they're committed to their two percent target and we can't get inflation under three.
The stock market, the S&P was up 2 and a half percent, and 10 year yields were up 30 basis points in the same week.
I've been one that's argued that 5% yield is fine, that the economy's fine with it, I even would argue the housing market's fine with it, and the stock market's fine with it.
If the data was more consistent and more dovish for the Fed, you know, quieter inflation that would suggest that they don't need to move, I think that that premium would go away.

key_points.point: The Fed faces a new era of uncertainty with divided opinions among policymakers and conflicting economic data.
Task forces created by the Fed will likely just reiterate what officials already know.
Other central banks like the Bank of England have had split votes without disrupting market expectations.
Current market uncertainty stems from conflicting data as well as lack of clear Fedspeak.
If economic data were more consistently dovish and showed quieter inflation, term premium would likely disappear.
key_points.condition: if data was more consistent and dovish

key_points.point: The economy, housing market, and stock market can function well with 5 percent yields.
Demand for compute and AI buildout will cause computing and chip demand to skyrocket over the next couple of years.
A successful IPO will come to market without creating major market hiccups.
